title: Checkout candidate comparison under a synthetic 20 requests/second workload
question: Under the declared synthetic workload and hard constraints, which checkout candidate should be preferred before a measured pilot?
context: Three candidates are compared with the same arrival rate, duration, warmup, metric definitions and seed scheme. Candidate A exposes a synchronous path with a short deadline and no retry budget. Candidate B uses a bounded queue, a longer deadline and a small retry budget. Candidate C adds servers but also coordination cost and a slower mean service time. The comparison is a conditional model result, not a production measurement.

constraints.statement: Every offered request must be completed, rejected, failed or still in the system; conservation must hold.
No candidate may silently drop a request without recording a rejection or failure.
The candidate must remain operable by the existing team without a new platform dependency; simulation cannot establish this condition.
Synthetic cost per 1000 successful requests must not exceed 3.0 relative cost units.
Synthetic 95th-percentile successful-request latency must not exceed 1.5 seconds.

candidates.title: Partitioned capacity with higher unit cost

outcome.rationale: Under the declared synthetic workload, candidate B has the highest success rate (0.9996, 95% CI 0.9995-0.9997) and the lowest cost per 1000 successful requests (1.34, 95% CI 1.33-1.34). Candidate A succeeds on 0.9218 of offered requests (95% CI 0.9211-0.9226) with a lower p95 latency of 0.870 s but a higher cost of 1.81 and a 7.8% timeout rate. Candidate C exceeds both the declared cost constraint at 3.63 and the p95 constraint at 1.769 s, and its success rate is 0.9679. Candidate B therefore dominates on the declared quantitative constraints. The recommendation is conditional: it does not establish production behavior, and the non-quantitative operability constraint C3 remains unverified.
non_quantitative_constraints: C3 operability by the existing team is not established by simulation and requires an explicit operational review.
The cost model is synthetic and relative; no currency amount or vendor price is implied.

reversal_triggers: A measured arrival rate above 22 requests/second or a measured mean service time above 0.65 seconds changes the utilization boundary.
A measured p95 service time whose tail causes B to exceed the 1.5-second latency constraint in the target environment.
A revised cost weight under which B no longer beats A on cost per successful request.
Failure of the C3 operability review or of a required platform dependency.
A measured retry rate that makes the 1.003 retry amplification materially larger than the modeled value.
limitations: All inputs are synthetic and uncalibrated; no production trace was used.
The confidence intervals use a normal approximation across 30 replications.
The model does not represent dependency calls, data consistency or network retries inside the service.
The sensitivity screen is a quadratic response-surface approximation, not a full pick-freeze Sobol analysis.

constraint_evaluation.evidence: All ten stored runs report invariants.conservation_ok true; the engine aborts on a failed invariant.
The discrete-event model records rejection, timeout and failure paths; no silent-drop path exists in the engine.
Operability by the existing team is a non-quantitative condition that requires a separate operational review.
Recommended candidate B is 1.34, A is 1.81, and C is 3.63; C is eliminated by the 3.0 ceiling.
A is 0.870 s and B is 1.206 s, within the 1.5-second ceiling; C is 1.769 s and is eliminated.
